normal_bowel_variability: Several bowel movements per day may be normal

acute_constipation.clinical_note: Requires careful assessment when sudden, severe, or associated with alarm symptoms

chronic_constipation.general_definition: Persistent constipation symptoms over weeks to months
chronic_constipation.rome_style_duration: Symptoms for at least 3 months with onset at least 6 months before diagnosis
chronic_constipation.broader_definition: Unsatisfactory defecation for at least 3 of the previous 12 months

stool_frequency: Fewer than three stools per week

duration_requirement: Criteria fulfilled for the last 3 months
Symptom onset at least 6 months before diagnosis
required_symptoms: Straining during at least 25% of defecations
Lumpy or hard stools in at least 25% of defecations
Sensation of incomplete evacuation in at least 25% of defecations
Sensation of anorectal obstruction or blockage in at least 25% of defecations
Manual maneuvers to facilitate at least 25% of defecations
Fewer than 3 spontaneous bowel movements per week
exclusion_features: Loose stools rarely present without laxatives
Insufficient criteria for irritable bowel syndrome

broader_clinical_definition.description: Unsatisfactory defecation characterized by infrequent stools, difficult stool passage, or both
broader_clinical_definition.chronic_duration: At least three of the previous twelve months

common_misconceptions: Belief that one bowel movement per day is always necessary
Concern about stool appearance despite normal variation
Assumption that less frequent stool always means disease
clinical_importance: Clarify the patient’s meaning of constipation
Separate stool frequency from stool passage difficulty

prevalence.general_population_range: Reported prevalence varies widely depending on definition and survey method
prevalence.older_surveys: 2% to 12.8% in some adult population surveys
prevalence.meta_analysis_global_estimate: Around 14% pooled prevalence of chronic constipation in adults
prevalence.rome_iii_estimate: Around 7% when stricter Rome III criteria are used
prevalence.adult_review_estimate: Around 16% worldwide in adults, with wide reported range
prevalence.older_adult_estimate: Higher prevalence in older adults, reported around one-third in some elderly groups

age: Older adults often have more medication and mobility-related risk
sex: Women report constipation more often than men in many studies
Rectal evacuation disorders are more frequent in women in several datasets
Rectal prolapse is more common in elderly women
healthcare_impact: Common reason for primary care visits
May require specialist testing when refractory
quality_of_life: Can cause anxiety about bowel function

normal_transit_constipation.definition: Constipation symptoms despite normal stool movement through the colon
response_pattern: Usually managed initially in primary care

slow_transit_constipation.definition: Delayed movement of stool through the colon
features: Poor response to simple measures in some cases

rectal_evacuation_disorder.definition: Difficulty evacuating stool from the rectum due to functional or structural outlet problems

opioids: Compound products such as co-codamol or co-dydramol

Do not stop medicines without clinician advice
Consider dose adjustment or alternatives under supervision
Use preventive bowel regimen when high-risk drugs are required

Persistent rectal bleeding without anal symptoms

overview.short_definition: Constipation means infrequent bowel movements, hard or lumpy stools, difficult stool passage, straining, or a feeling that stool has not fully passed.
overview.simple_explanation: Constipation happens when stool moves too slowly through the colon, becomes too dry, or cannot be passed properly due to pelvic floor or outlet problems.
common_in: People with neurological, endocrine, or metabolic diseases
main_types: Secondary constipation due to medicine, disease, obstruction, or metabolic cause

classification.description: Stool movement through the colon is normal, but the person feels constipated or has difficulty passing stool.
classification.chatbot_note: Often improves with fiber, water, exercise, and osmotic laxatives.

classification.description: Stool moves slowly through the colon, causing hard, dry, small, or infrequent stools.
classification.chatbot_note: May need laxatives and specialist testing if persistent.

classification.description: The rectum or pelvic floor does not relax or coordinate properly during bowel movement.
classification.chatbot_note: Symptoms include long straining, incomplete evacuation, manual maneuvers, or difficulty passing even soft stool. Biofeedback is often useful.

classification.description: Constipation caused by medicines, mechanical obstruction, metabolic disease, neurological disease, myopathy, or psychological conditions.
classification.chatbot_note: Needs review of medicines and possible medical evaluation.

rome_style_symptom_criteria.duration: Symptoms are generally considered chronic when present for several months.
features: Feeling of blockage in the anus or rectum
Need for manual help to pass stool
Fewer than 3 bowel movements per week
rome_style_symptom_criteria.ib_s_note: If recurrent abdominal pain is a dominant symptom and linked to stool changes, IBS-C may need to be considered.

common: Fewer than 3 bowel movements per week
Need to sit for a long time in toilet
Need for finger or hand support to pass stool
outlet_obstruction_suggestive: Feeling stool is stuck near anus
Need to press around vagina or perineum
fecal_impaction_suggestive: No bowel movement for several days
Feeling of stool stuck in rectum

red_flags.red_flag: Blood in stool or rectal bleeding
New or worsening constipation, especially in older adults
Family history of colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease
Cannot pass gas with abdominal swelling

history_questions: How many bowel movements do you have per week?
Is stool hard, lumpy, or painful?
Do you feel blockage near the anus?
Any weight loss, fever, vomiting, or severe pain?
What medicines or supplements are you taking?
How much water do you drink?
How much fiber do you eat?
Any thyroid, diabetes, kidney, neurological, or colon disease?
physical_exam: Abdominal exam for distension, tenderness, masses, or enlarged organs
Perineal exam for fissures, hemorrhoids, skin tags, or warts
Rectal exam for stool, tone, masses, rectocele, and pelvic floor movement

possible_tests.reason: Check anemia or infection if clinically needed.
Check hypothyroidism when symptoms suggest it.
Needed with alarm features or age/risk-based colorectal cancer screening.
Evaluate defecatory disorder when incomplete evacuation or outlet symptoms persist.
Assess ability to expel stool-like balloon.
Evaluate slow transit constipation when anorectal testing is normal or symptoms are refractory.
Assess rectocele, prolapse, intussusception, or dyssynergia when needed.

first_line_lifestyle: Drink adequate fluids unless medically restricted
Walk or do regular physical activity
Do not ignore urge to pass stool
Try toilet sitting after meals to use gastrocolic reflex
Use footstool to improve squatting posture

fiber_guidance.target: About 20 to 30 grams per day for many adults, increased gradually.
fiber_guidance.caution: Increase slowly to avoid gas and bloating.

medicine_options_to_discuss_with_clinici.note: Draws water into bowel to soften stool.
Can be useful but should be used appropriately.
May help some people, but effect can be limited.

examples: Secretagogues or prokinetic agents depending on country/clinician
medicine_options_to_discuss_with_clinici.note: Used for persistent chronic constipation under medical advice.

defecatory_disorder_management: Relaxation of pelvic floor during defecation

hydration: Warm water in morning if helpful
Oral fluids unless restricted by kidney, heart, or other medical condition

sample_day_plan.midday: Dal or beans with vegetables and whole grain.
